where the scholiast has γρ. τυφόμενον [variant reading: smoldering], οἷον καιόμενον πολεμίῳ πυρί [that is, burning with hostile fire]. If τυφόμενον [smoldering] is written, στράτευμ' [the army] would have to be changed to στρατόν [the army]. But it seems to be nothing other than a gloss on the word άπτομενον [kindling], although it is strange that this is said of men: for this reason Prien conjectured καὶ στρατοῦ δαπτομέναν πυρὶ δαΐῳ [and the army being consumed by hostile fire].

that is, wrath aroused because of unburnt sacrifices. Blomfield explained it almost this way in his Glossary p. 160, refuting the scholiast's interpretation of the sacrifices of the Fates and the Furies, which are also called νηφάλια [wineless offerings]. Hesychius noted that ἀπύρου [without fire] is used for ἀθύτου [without sacrifice] from Sophocles (fr. 366).

Schol. on οἴστρου δ᾽ ἄρδις [the goad's point]: the point of fire. ἄπυρος [without fire]: either (correct to or) πολύπυρος [much fire] (if the a is intensive) because of the violence of the passion, or having no fire. The second interpretation is the true one. He adds ἄπυρος [without fire] to indicate that it is used improperly.

therefore, and so. It is a syllogistic conjunction, as Ammonius p. 28 and other grammarians teach, and it retains its syllogistic force, although the Latin particles igitur or itaque are not always suitable to express it.
where Victorius rightly deleted ἄρ' [then], which I restored in the next line, ἄρα σ' ἐγώ [then I you], for τάδ᾽ ἐγώσε [these things I to you].
Likewise it retains its syllogistic force in interrogative sentences, for example
the sign-maker was not some cheap fellow, then.
